title: Given the root of a binary tree, return the values of the nodes you can see when looking at the tree from the right side, ordered from top to bottom.
shortTitle: Binary Tree Right Side View: BFS taking last node per level
keyPoints: The right side view is the last node of each level in a breadth-first traversal, not just the right spine
Use BFS with the level-size snapshot: snapshot queue size, drain that many nodes, capture the last one
Enqueue left before right so nodes are processed left-to-right within each level
A left node can appear in the right view if there is no right node at that level
The DFS alternative visits right before left and records the first node at each new depth
Time is O(n), space is O(w) where w is the maximum width of the tree

s1_definition.oneliner: Do a level-order traversal and record the last node of each level, which is the rightmost one visible from the right.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Right side view** – the set of nodes visible when standing on the right side of a binary tree, which is the last node per level top to bottom.
- **BFS with level-size snapshot** – capture `queue.size()` at the start of each level, drain that many nodes, and record the one at index `levelSize - 1`.
- **Not the right spine** – the rightmost node per level may come from the left subtree if the right side is shorter.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time (each node enqueued and dequeued once), O(w) space for the queue.
- **DFS alternative** – visit right child first, record the first node seen at each new depth.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine standing to the right of the National Bank of India's approval hierarchy and seeing only the person furthest to the right on each rank. The top manager is visible, then on the next rank only the rightmost report is visible because the others are hidden behind them, and so on down the chart.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  BFS Level-Size Snapshot

       CEO          Level 0: [CEO]       → right view: CEO
      /   \
    VP1   VP2       Level 1: [VP1, VP2]  → right view: VP2
   /
  DIR1              Level 2: [DIR1]      → right view: DIR1

  Right view: [CEO, VP2, DIR1]
  Note: DIR1 is a left child but visible from the right
```

```text
  DFS Right-First Alternative

  Visit order: CEO(depth 0) → VP2(depth 1) → VP1(depth 1, skip)
               → DIR1(depth 2)

  result.size() at each new depth:
    depth 0: size=0, add CEO    → [CEO]
    depth 1: size=1, add VP2    → [CEO, VP2]
    depth 1: size=2, skip VP1   (already have depth 1)
    depth 2: size=2, add DIR1   → [CEO, VP2, DIR1]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The right side view of a binary tree is the last node of each level, which is what you would see standing on the right side. You compute it with BFS and the level-size snapshot: enqueue the root, snapshot the queue size at the start of each level, drain that many nodes, and capture the one at index `levelSize - 1`. Children are enqueued left then right so nodes process in the correct order.

The crucial subtlety is that the right view is not the right spine. A left node can appear in the view if the right subtree does not extend to that depth. Tracking the last node per level handles this automatically, while naively following only right children would miss deeper left-side nodes.

The DFS alternative visits the right child first and records the first node seen at each new depth. It uses less memory on wide trees because its space is proportional to height rather than width. The symmetric left view captures the first node per level instead of the last.

In our banking system at National Bank of India, the right view builds an emergency contact sheet showing the most senior fallback at each escalation level. Some levels have a missing right branch, so the visible contact is a left-side node, and the level-based last-node rule correctly includes those fallbacks.

Remember one sentence: BFS level-size snapshot capturing the last node per level gives the right view, which is not just the right spine.
